newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen steady in Pakistan, up in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen steady in Pakistan, up in India.

text.p: Cotton rates are likely to remain steady in Pakistan next week amid select buying by mill owners and exporters, while in India rates could gain on a shortage of ready stocks, dealers said on Friday.
In Pakistan, fresh buying boosted rates last week as the 1996/97 (July-June) season drew to a close, but dealers said the trend might change as prices were now beyond buyers' reach.
"There was buying yesterday, but today trading remained dull as the rates are too high," dealer Nasim Usman said.

"Current cotton rates are unsuitable for exporters, while mill owners are also finding them high. But as there is not much cotton available from 1996/97 crop, they would go for good quality stocks," he added.
Dealers said the ginners had no more than 450,000 bales of unsold cotton left from the 1996/97 crop.
Usman said sellers were likely to hold their positions as the arrival of the 1997/98 crop might be delayed.
"In Punjab province, fresh supplies will be delayed because of rains, while in Sindh province, bad weather could also slow down the arrival of new supplies," he said.
The Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association has said 1996/97 cotton output reached a provisional 8.78 million 375-lb bales by June 1, down from 9.938 million at the same time a year ago.

India is expected to harvest a record cotton crop of around 16.7 million 170-kg bales in the 1996/97 (October-September) season, up from 16.27 million previous year, traders said.
They said most cotton-producing states had reported higher production following good weather conditions.
Maharashtra and Gujarat in western India harvested 5.0 million bales and 3.5 million respectively in 1996/97 after the previous year's 4.5 million and 3.2 million, traders said.
A national conference of trade organisations affiliated to the East India Cotton Association (EICA) are meeting in Bombay on Saturday to estimate the 1996/97 crop.
The meeting is also expected to discuss impending futures trading in cotton and the need to set up a technology mission to raise productivity, traders said.
The 1997/98 (April/March) federal budget proposed reintroducing cotton futures trading after a gap of 30 years.
Futures trading in cotton and other key commodities was banned in the early 1960s to curb speculation and stabilise prices.
An official committee, set up to suggest a mechanism to implement futures trading in cotton, is expected to submit its report shortly, traders said.

Low productivity in cotton has been a major worry for farmers and the government. The average Indian cotton yield of about 310 kgs per hectare is far below the world average of 570 kgs, let alone Australia's 1,300 kgs per hectare.
Cotton prices made further gains this week due to falling arrivals as the season winds down. Most of the crop harvested in the 1996/97 season will have arrived by July, traders said.
A shortage of ready stock also pushed up cotton prices on the Bombay market, they said.

"Demand from cotton and yarn mills had been dull but as prices started rising they turned active buyers," said Mahesh Thakkar, a leading dealer. "Most spinning mills have secured export orders for cotton yarn and these are buying up quality cotton at any price to meet their commitments."

In spot, Punjab saw-ginned rose 55 rupees to 1,830/1,900 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and F-414 gained 25/30 rupees to 2,040/2,060 rupees per maund. Bengal-deshi moved up by 70/80 rupees to 1,050/1,080 rupees per maund.
"We are witnessing a shortage of good quality cotton due to the...end of the season," one trader said.
Blenders too remained active buyers in the average and medium quality, he said.
Long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 rose 1,500/2,000 rupees to 19,000/23,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg). Medium-staple Gujarat Kalyan lost 200 rupees to 14,300/14,800 rupees per candy.
